summary: Space hardware can fail in ways that small validation errors make worse, so teams test equipment at Earth sites that reproduce some planetary conditions. No Earth site is a full twin of the Moon or Mars, and sites that look valid can carry hidden terrestrial factors that produce false positives. Ixmati ranks Earth analog sites against a chosen lunar or Martian location for one engineering test at a time. Users pick one of three missions: mobility, navigation, or environmental survival. For each target and mission, the platform returns the three closest Earth sites, a per-variable breakdown, a robustness analysis, and an extrapolation report that lists the target conditions no Earth site reproduces. The tool connects planetary GIS data with an interface aimed at university and emerging engineering teams. Across 90 target-mission combinations, the top-ranked site changes with the mission in 25 cases, which supports analog selection being specific to each test. Catalog values are compiled estimates, and only 149 of 1,104 non-empty values are confirmed against official sources, so the results should be read as a prototype.
details:
What it does and how it works. Ixmati helps engineering teams choose where to test lunar and Martian equipment on Earth. The user picks a Moon or Mars region and one of three missions: mobility, navigation (perception), or environmental survival. The backend ranks Earth analog sites by similarity and returns the three closest, with a per-variable breakdown, a robustness analysis, and an extrapolation report that lists which target conditions no Earth site can reproduce. The method uses 25 variables grouped into seven physical categories. Mission weights are derived from each variable’s category mix and the mission’s demand profile, using a Kullback–Leibler allocation, so the weights are not hand-tuned per variable. Distances are weighted Euclidean, with coverage reporting for missing data and projection of out-of-range targets onto the Earth range.

Benefits. The same target gives different analogs for different tests, so a team can match the site to the activity it is testing. The results are auditable: every match includes its full data, the weight report, and a stability analysis under 200 perturbed mission profiles. Across 90 target-mission combinations, the best analog stays the top choice in 94.9% of trials on average.

Intended impact. The platform is aimed at university and early-stage engineering teams, who often build rovers and test in field campaigns and need to know both where to test and what the test will fail to reproduce. The extrapolation report is meant to prevent false confidence from analog tests, a failure mode documented in past missions such as Spirit and InSight HP³.

Tools and technologies. Backend: Go, standard library only. Frontend: plain ES modules with Three.js 0.164.1 and no build step. Data: Python scripts (fetch_earth_apis.py, raster_tools.py) that extract values from NASA POWER, MODIS, SRTM, LOLA, and MOLA. Tests: go test and Python test scripts. The team used Claude (Anthropic) for code, mathematics, tests, and drafting, and reviewed and ran all of it.

Creativity. The mission weights come from a mathematical derivation rather than manual tuning. The project also reports where Earth cannot reproduce a target, rather than hiding it, and it turns a mission-driven 3D interface into a way of exploring analogs.

Factors considered. Safety of input (the planet and region names are validated against a whitelist, so user input never builds a file path), data provenance (every value is classified into tiers A, B, C, or estimate, with 149 of 1,104 values confirmed against official sources), known analog failures in past missions, and the honest reporting of missing data and limitations.
